title: Behavioral, senior technical program manager, strong answers, tough

questions.text: Tell me about a program you drove across several teams.
Tell me about a time two teams disagreed on priorities and you had to resolve it.
Tell me about a program that slipped or failed.
Tell me about explaining a serious risk to executives.
Tell me about mentoring someone on your team.
Tell me about a process change that other teams adopted.

persona.pushback_style: challenges choices with the simpler alternative

brief.curveball: Suppose your sponsor is out for two weeks and two teams refuse to move on a shared deadline. What do you do?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Hello Imani, thank you for joining. I'm Julian, a director of program management. This is a forty-five minute behavioral interview, and I will push on your choices.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Hello Julian, thank you. I'm glad to be here.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Have you been in program management for a long time?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: About nine years, the last five leading cross-team programs.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Good. I'll cover four experiences, then there is time for your questions.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about a program you drove across several teams.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I led our payment platform migration across nine teams and about 60 engineers over fourteen months. I built the dependency map, ran a weekly cross-team review, and set a rule that no team could cut over without a tested rollback. I was accountable for the schedule and the risk log. We moved all traffic with zero customer-facing outages and finished two weeks early. I handed the weekly review to a senior engineer in month ten, so the program did not depend on me.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How did you decide the order in which teams moved?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I ranked teams by the risk of the service and how ready the team was. I moved low-risk, ready teams first so we could learn on small traffic. Billing, the riskiest, went last. Two teams wanted to go early for prestige, and I said no, using data from the first three cutovers: a rollback took 40 minutes the first time and 8 minutes by the third.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about a time two teams disagreed on priorities and you had to resolve it.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: The fraud team and the checkout team both needed the same three engineers from the shared platform group in the same quarter. Each had a good case, and I did not pick a side. I asked each lead for the value at stake. Fraud's number was 2.1 million dollars in avoided losses against 1.4 million in checkout revenue. I split the work so checkout got one engineer plus a contractor. Both leads signed the plan, and both hit their dates.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Why not just escalate to your director and let her decide? That is simpler.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I considered it. Escalation is fast, but both leads would have lost trust in each other and in me, and I would have needed to ask her again next quarter. Using their own numbers took three days instead of one, and it gave them a way to settle it themselves. They did: the same two leads agreed on the next quarter's split without me.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about a program that slipped or failed.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: An analytics data platform I ran slipped by three months. I had trusted one team's estimate without checking their dependencies, and an unplanned security review added eight weeks. I told my sponsor as soon as I saw it, with a recovery plan, and cut scope to the three reports customers used most. We landed with 80 percent of scope and kept the key customer. Since then I check dependencies on every estimate, and I put a security review into every plan at the start.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Suppose your sponsor is out for two weeks and two teams refuse to move on a shared deadline. What do you do?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: First I would find out why they refuse, because it is usually a real constraint. Then I would put the deadline and each team's cost on one page and bring it to their two managers instead of waiting for the sponsor. If it is a true conflict, I would ask for a delegate from the sponsor's staff. A similar case in my migration was settled in two days this way. I would also message the sponsor so there are no surprises.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about a process change that other teams adopted.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I introduced a one page launch readiness checklist. I tested it with two teams first and cut it from 30 items to 12 after they said it was too long. Then I showed that launches using it had 45 percent fewer rollbacks over two quarters. Eleven teams adopted it, mostly because their engineers asked for it, not because I required it.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Thank you. What questions do you have for me?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: How do program managers here share what works across organizations?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: We have a monthly review where two programs present lessons, and the notes go into a shared playbook.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That's our time. Thanks Imani, the recruiter will follow up within a week.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Thank you, Julian.

notes: Strong for senior: cross-team scope, numbers, trade-offs. Handles pushback and the curveball well.
